title: Why big fierce animals are rare
teaches: How energy passes up a food chain, why most of it ends as heat, and why that keeps chains short and top predators few

parts.title: A young man and a bog lake

blocks.text: Cedar Bog Lake, north of Minneapolis, is small and shallow: a few acres of open water, nowhere much deeper than a tall person, slowly filling in with peat and turning into bog. In the late 1930s a graduate student at the University of Minnesota, Raymond Lindeman, chose it for his doctorate. With his wife Eleanor, he spent several years sampling everything that lived in it, through all seasons, including through holes in the winter ice: the algae and water plants, the tiny animals that ate them, the insect larvae and fish that ate those, and the bacteria in the ooze at the bottom.

Ecologists before him had described food chains: who eats whom. Lindeman wanted to measure them. He converted every sample into the energy it contained, in calories, and asked how much energy flowed from each **trophic level**, or feeding level, to the next: from sunlight to plants, plants to plant-eaters, plant-eaters to meat-eaters. It was a new way to look at a lake, as a machine that energy runs through.

In 1941 he went to Yale to work with G. Evelyn Hutchinson, and wrote the results up as a short, bold paper. The journal *Ecology* turned it down: its reviewers thought it too theoretical, built on too little data. Hutchinson argued for it, and it was accepted. By then Lindeman was seriously ill with liver disease. He died in June 1942, aged 26, a few months before “The trophic-dynamic aspect of ecology” appeared. It became one of the most cited papers in the subject.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Raymond Lindeman measured the energy in every level of Cedar Bog Lake's food chain in the late 1930s.
His 1942 paper treated a lake as energy flowing through **trophic levels**, or feeding levels.

blocks.text: Lindeman's lake began with sunlight. The algae and water plants captured only a tiny fraction of what fell on the lake, about a tenth of one percent, and stored it as sugar and the other substances of their bodies. (How they do it is the subject of the first lessons of the Botany course.) Everything else in the lake ran on that.

Then he followed it up. Of all the energy stored in the plants over a year, only a small part ended up stored in the bodies of the animals that ate them. Of that, again only a part reached the meat-eaters. In his numbers each step passed on somewhere between a tenth and a fifth. Ecologists later turned this into a rule of thumb: roughly **a tenth** of the energy at one level reaches the next. Real values run from two percent to about a quarter, depending on who is eating whom.

blocks.caption: An energy pyramid: what each level stores in a year, with a set share passed up at each step. Widths to scale. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a share that keeps five levels alive

blocks.text: At a tenth per step, ten thousand units of plant become a thousand of plant-eater, a hundred of meat-eater, and ten of whatever eats meat-eaters. Drawn to scale, as in the figure, the levels shrink so fast that the fourth is a sliver. This is the **energy pyramid**, and it is why there are many more rabbits than foxes, and more foxes than eagles.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Plants capture a small fraction of sunlight; each step up the chain passes on only a share of what it gets.
As a rule of thumb, about a tenth passes up each step; real values run from 2 to 25 percent.
So each level holds far less energy than the one below: the **energy pyramid**.

blocks.text: If nine tenths of the energy doesn't pass up, where does it go? Some of the plant is never eaten: it dies and rots. Some that is eaten isn't digested and leaves as droppings. Both go to the decomposers, the bacteria and fungi that Lindeman found in the ooze, which run their own lives on it. But most of the energy an animal does digest, it burns.

Every living thing spends energy staying alive: pumping blood, moving, keeping its cells in repair, and for birds and mammals, keeping warm. All of it ends as heat, which leaves the animal and in the end radiates off into space. A big warm-blooded hunter like a lion turns only a few percent at most of the meat it eats into new lion; the rest keeps it warm and running. A spider or a fish, cold-blooded and slow, can turn ten percent or more of its food into body. That is why chains of warm-blooded animals are especially steep.

Heat can't be used again to grow a plant or power a muscle. So energy passes through a food web once, from sunlight to heat, and doesn't come back. A lake or a forest keeps running only because the Sun keeps shining on it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Most energy that isn't passed up is burned to stay alive, and leaves as heat.
Warm-blooded animals burn the most, so they pass on the least.
Energy passes through an ecosystem once, from sunlight to heat, and is not recycled.

blocks.text: A predator needs more than a trickle of energy. It needs enough prey, in a small enough area, to find a meal before it starves, and enough of its own kind nearby to find a mate. At each level up the chain, there is less to go round. Somewhere around the fourth or fifth level there isn't enough left to support a population of anything. That is the answer the ecologist Paul Colinvaux gave in 1978 in his book *Why Big Fierce Animals Are Rare*: there just isn't enough energy at the top.

It is also why top predators range so widely. A wolf pack in Yellowstone patrols hundreds of square kilometres; a tiger may need a hundred square kilometres to itself. They aren't greedy. The energy that reaches them has been thinned at every step, and they have to gather it from a huge area.

Ecologists still argue over whether energy alone sets the length of food chains. Some of the most productive places on Earth, such as tropical forests, don't have noticeably longer chains than poorer ones, and big lakes tend to have longer chains than small lakes no matter how productive they are. Size, disturbance and history matter too. But energy sets the outer limit: no amount of history can put a sixth level on a chain that can feed only four.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: After four or five levels there isn't enough energy left to support another population.
Top predators are rare and range widely because the energy reaching them is thin.
Energy sets the limit; other things, such as a habitat's size, affect how close chains get to it.

blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. In a forest, the mass of the trees vastly outweighs the deer and caterpillars, which outweigh the wolves and birds: a pyramid of mass, the right way up. But in the open ocean, the weight of all the floating algae in a patch of sea at a given moment can be *less* than the weight of the tiny animals eating them. How can the eaters outweigh their food, if energy shrinks at each step?

blocks.caption: A patch of sea: algae, the small animals that eat them, and fish. What stands in the water at any moment depends on how much each level makes in a year and how long it lasts. A model.
blocks.task: Make the algae short-lived, then compare with what each level makes in a year

blocks.text: The answer is speed. An ocean alga is a single cell that divides every day or two, and is eaten almost as fast as it grows. A tree lasts for centuries. So at any moment there is little algae standing in the water, but over a year it makes an enormous amount. The pyramid of *mass at one moment* can stand on its point; the pyramid of *energy made in a year* never can. Lindeman's insight was to measure the flow, not the stock, and the flow is always a pyramid.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: In the open sea, fast-growing, short-lived algae can weigh less at any moment than the animals eating them.
The pyramid of energy made per year is always the right way up.

blocks.text: Energy and matter behave differently in an ecosystem, and the difference is worth holding on to. The carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus in a rabbit came from the plants it ate. When the rabbit dies, or is eaten and the fox dies, decomposers break the bodies down and release those atoms back into the soil, water and air, where plants take them up again. The same atoms can go round and round for millions of years.

Energy can't. It enters as sunlight, moves up the chain getting smaller at each step, and leaves as heat. So a garden, a lake or a forest is like a waterwheel: the matter is the wheel, turning round and round, and the energy is the water that drives it, falling through once. Later lessons follow the wheel: carbon round the whole planet, and nitrogen through a forest that was cut down on purpose to see where it would go.

One practical consequence comes from the energy pyramid. An acre of wheat eaten as bread feeds several times more people than the same acre's wheat fed to cattle and eaten as beef, because cattle, warm-blooded and large, burn most of what they eat. How much more depends on the animal and the farm, but it is never fewer.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Matter goes round: decomposers return atoms to soil, water and air, to be used again.
Energy goes through: in as sunlight, out as heat.
Eating lower on the chain feeds more people from the same land.

blocks.caption: Six questions on energy
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A meadow's plants store 50,000 units of energy in a year. With about a tenth passed up at each step, about how much reaches the hawks that eat the snakes that eat the mice?
items.why: Mice get about 5,000, snakes about 500, hawks about 50. Three steps, each passing on a tenth.

items.ask: Of the energy a fox digests, where does most of it end up?
choices: As heat, from keeping warm and moving
items.why: Most digested energy is burned to stay alive and leaves as heat, which can't be used again.

items.ask: Why do top predators such as wolves need such large areas?
choices: The energy reaching their level is spread thin over a large area
They are territorial for no reason
There are too many of them
items.why: Each level gets only a share of the one below, so the energy available at the top is small per square kilometre.

items.ask: In the open sea, the floating algae in a patch of water at one moment can weigh less than the animals eating them. How?
choices: The algae grow and are eaten very fast, so little stands at any moment
Energy increases up the chain in the sea
items.why: Algae divide every day or two. Over a year they make far more than the animals do, even if little is there at any instant.

items.ask: Which of these goes round and round in an ecosystem, and which passes through once?
choices: Matter goes round; energy passes through
Energy goes round; matter passes through
items.why: Decomposers return atoms to be used again, but energy ends as heat, which can't drive living things again.

items.ask: A food chain's animals are all cold-blooded insects and spiders instead of birds and mammals. What would you expect?
choices: More energy passed up each step, so the chain can support more
Less energy passed up each step
items.why: Cold-blooded animals don't burn food to keep warm, so they turn a bigger share of what they eat into body for the next level.

summary: **Lindeman followed energy through Cedar Bog Lake.** His 1942 paper, published after his death at 26, treated an ecosystem as energy flowing through feeding levels.
**Each step up a food chain passes on only a share.** Roughly a tenth, as a rule of thumb; really from 2 to 25 percent.
**Most of the rest ends as heat.** Burned to keep alive, warm and moving, and lost for good.
**Warm-blooded animals pass on least.** A lion turns only a few percent at most of its food into new lion.
**So food chains are short and top predators rare.** After four or five levels there isn't enough energy left.
**Pyramids of mass can stand on their point.** Fast-growing ocean algae can weigh less at any moment than the animals eating them; the energy made each year is always a pyramid.
**Matter goes round; energy goes through.** Atoms are reused for ever; energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.
